name: Boxing
tagline: Two fists, twelve rounds, and the sweet science of distance.
overview: Boxing is a fistfight with laws: two opponents in padded gloves trade punches within a roped square over timed rounds, winning by knockout, by judges' decision, or by the referee's stoppage. Beneath the violence lies the most studied striking art in history — footwork, feints, ring geometry, and the economy of the jab — earning the sport its old name, the sweet science.

The Queensberry Rules (1867) ended bare-knuckle's lawless era and created modern boxing: three-minute rounds, padded gloves, and ten counts. Olympic since 1904, professional since before living memory, boxing produced sport's first global superstars and its most mythic narratives — Ali's exile and return, Louis's crosses of America, Hagler-Hearms wars — and it remains, alongside football and athletics, one of the only sports where one dramatic night can rewrite a life.

Newcomers should learn stance, jab, and footwork before ever dreaming of hooks: boxing is fought from the legs, and six months of bag work and shadow boxing build the base that makes sparring productive. Find a gym with a coach, buy wraps and gloves, and respect the sport's first rule — protect yourself at all times, including from the enthusiasm of beginners.

Slip-rope drills daily; partner-feeder defense rounds; defensive-only sparring (light contact, defense scores).

Three-minute intervals with one-minute rests, at fight pace, forever: the round is the sport's true unit.
Round-based bag and pad circuits; roadwork with intervals; neck and core strength for taking and absorbing clean.

Controlled sparring with goals (survive a round center-ring, box the outside, work off the jab); fight-film study per opponent archetype.
rules: Scoring: ten-point must — the round's winner takes 10, the loser 9 (8 after a knockdown; 10-10 for even rounds).

Legal targets: above the belt, front and sides of head and body; rabbit punches, kidney shots, and holding-and-hitting draw warnings and point deductions.
Clinching: holding without punching draws breaks; excessive holding is penalized.

name: Wrestling
tagline: The oldest sport in the Olympic record — take them down, turn them, pin them.
overview: Wrestling is human chess at body temperature: two athletes seek takedowns, turns, and pins — or points for control, exposure, and escapes — under rules that forbid striking but permit nearly everything else two bodies can do. It was on the ancient Olympic program by 708 BC, it anchors every modern Games since 1896, and its styles (freestyle, Greco-Roman, and America's folkstyle) form the technical base of most grappling sports on Earth.

The modern international game is governed by United World Wrestling (founded 1912 as FILA) with six weight classes per style per sex at the Olympics. The sport's deepest nations — Iran, Russia's lineage, the USA, Japan (whose women's program is the most dominant in Olympic wrestling history), and the Caucasus — treat wrestling as civic identity, and its legends (Karelin's thirteen years without a single point conceded in international competition, Icho's four golds, Gable's perfection) are national monuments.

Newcomers should learn sprawls, stance, and level changes before throws: wrestling rewards position over heroics, and the safest entry is a club with structured drilling. conditioning is the sport's honest tax — six minutes of wrestling feels like an hour of running — and every takedown you learn transfers to judo, BJJ, and MMA.

The wrestling stance: knees bent, back straight, head up, always moving — level changes create every attack.
Stance-and-motion drills (5-minute continuous motion); level-change repetitions by the hundred; mirror and video checks weekly.

Penetration-step repetitions (50 daily); finish ladders against resistance; chain-wrestling drills (miss-to-second-attack).

The sprawl that stuffs takedowns, whizzer replies, and front headlocks — defense first, always.
Sprawl reps by the hundred; defense-only drilling rounds; reactive drills with a partner calling shots.

The ground game: breakdowns, rides (bar-arm, half-nelson family), turns to pin combinations.
Position sparring from referees' positions; pin-combination chains drilled weekly; near-fall awareness (exposure points).
Throws (Greco & freestyle)
Lifts, hip throws, and suplayssuplexes: the sport's highlight scoring when landed cleanly.
Throw technique with crash pads; grip-and-lift strength (5×5 heavy); timing throws off opponent attacks.

Interval circuits (30 s on/15 s off × 12); live-wrestling rounds at full pace; weight managed by eating, not cutting (young athletes especially).

Scoring: takedown 2 (4-5 with exposure or grand amplitude throws), reversal 2, escape 1, near-fall/exposure 2-4; pins (both shouldersshoulder blades to the mat) end everything instantly.

Par terre/position restarts: after certain stoppages wrestlers restart in the ground position — the sport's built-in ground phase.
Caution points and passivity: referees enforce action; passivity warnings and cautions award points and position.
Weight classes: senior freestyle weights of 57, 65, 74, 86, 97, and 125 kg, same structure for Greco and women; weigh-ins the day before at majors.

Strength for the chain: deadlifts, rows, pull-ups, and neck work — wrestling strength is posterior-chain strength.

name: Judo
tagline: The gentle way — Kano's throws, pins, and the Olympic mat's moral curriculum.
overview: Judo — the gentle way — is Jigoro Kano's synthesis of Japanese jujutsu into a modern martial art and sport: throws (nage-waza) and grappling (katame-waza: pins, chokes, jointlocks) used to control an opponent by leveraging their balance against them. Kano's genius was pedagogical: he stripped dangerous techniques, built randori (free practice) at its heart, and wrapped the whole thing in a moral philosophy (jita kyoei — mutual benefit) that made judo the world's first modern martial art.

Founded at Tokyo's Kodokan in 1882, judo became the first martial art in the Olympics (Tokyo 1964, permanent from 1972) and the template for every modern grappling sport that followed — sambo, BJJ, and the pedagogy of most national combatives systems. The IJF's world circuit and the Olympic mat's seven weight classes per sex define elite judo, where a single throw for ippon ends the match instantly and cleanly.

Newcomers should start at a club with proper mats and instructors: falling (ukemi) is the sport's first and most important skill — taught before throws — and judo's learning curve is famously kind to beginners because you cannot learn to throw without learning to be thrown. Grip fighting, footwork, and one good throw beat a shallow arsenal of twenty.

Individual tournaments by weight class in single elimination with bronze-medal repêchage brackets, plus the mixed-team event since Tokyo 2020.
Kata

skills: Ukemi (falling)
The sport's first skill: breakfalls (back, side, forward) that make being thrown safe forever.
Daily ukemi from kneeling to standing; rolling fall progressions; falling is tested in every warm-up, forever.
Kumi-kata (grip fighting)
The invisible battle: obtaining your grip while denying theirs — the sport's opening chess.
Grip-breaking drills (high collar versus sleeve, two-on-one breaks); grip-only sparring rounds; hand speed and wrist strength work.
Throws (nage-waza)
The Kodokan's sixty-seven classic throws across hip, foot, hand, sacrifice families — learn three deeply before thirty shallowly.
Uchi-komi (repetition entries) by the hundred; nage-komi (throws onto crash mats); randori application of one tokui-waza (favorite throw).
Newaza (groundwork)
Pins (osaekomi), escapes, turns, chokes (shime-waza) and armlocks (kansetsu-waza, elbow only in sport).
Groundwork rounds starting from pin positions; turn-over technique chains; transition timing (throw-to-pin) drilled as one motion.
Combination & counters
Renraku-waza: throw-to-throw combinations and counters (kaeshi-waza) — the mature randori skill.
Combination drilling (attack-drives-attack); counter-of-the-month practice; situational randori with announced intentions.
Randori & competition craft
Free practice as the sport's laboratory: pace management, score awareness, and the last thirty seconds' discipline.
Structured randori with goals; tournament simulation with scoring rules enforced; shiai experience accumulated deliberately.

Prohibited: leg grabs (since 2010-2013 rules), direct attacks below the belt, and techniques judged dangerous (divingkani-basami banned).
Match time: four minutes senior with golden-score overtime; the rules' evolution is constant — check the current IJF sport code.
Uniform: IJF-approved judogi, regulated sizes, blue and white sets; belt ranks (kyu/dan) formalized by Kano himself.

Strength and conditioning: pulls (the grip game's engine), squats, and rotational power — judo strength is grip-and-hip strength.
Cross-train thoughtfully: wrestling makes judoka harder to throw; BJJ deepens the newaza; each borrows well.

name: Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu
tagline: Position before submission — the gentle art that rebuilt grappling for the ground.
overview: Brazilian jiu-jitsu is ground fighting as a science: control positions (guard, mount, back), sweeps, escapes, and submissions (chokes, joint locks) refined so a smaller, skilled practitioner can neutralize and defeat a larger one. Its premise — position before submission, technique over strength — made it the technical engine of mixed martial arts and one of the fastest-growing martial arts in the world.

The art descends from judo's groundwork (Kano's newaza and the Kosen university tradition) brought to Brazil by Mitsuyo Maeda, transformed by Carlos and Helio Gracie (Helio's leverage adaptations for a smaller frame), tested in the Gracie challenge matches, and globalized through the UFC's first event (1993) and Royce Gracie's wins. Today it splits into gi competition (IBJJF's worlds and the belt system) and no-gi grappling (ADCC's superfight crown), with academies in every city on Earth.

Newcomers should expect to be submitted daily for six months and to love it: BJJ's culture is built on controlled resistance, and its curriculum (positions before submissions) is the most teachable in grappling. Start with fundamentals classes, learn to tap early and often, and trust the belt system's long arc — blue belt takes about two years, and the journey is the point.

formats: Gi competition
IBJJF rules: points for takedown (2), sweep (2), guard pass (3), knee-on-belly mount and back (4); advantages, penalties, and submissions decide matches.
No-gi & ADCC-style
Gripless grappling with submission-only scoring variants; ADCC's points-plus-submission format is grappling's most prestigious stage.
Submission-only (EBI-style)
No points: matches decided by submission or overtime rounds (ride-outs and escape challenges) — the purist format.
Academy sport & in-house

skills: Guard & guard retention
The defining position: closed, open, and modern guards (De La Riva, worm, 50/50) that keep you dangerous from your back.
Guard retention drills (posture control, hip escapes); open-guard chaining by grip or leg entanglement; retention against pressure passing weekly.
Passing
Beating the guard: pressure passing (knee-cut, headquarters, and leg-drag) and speed passing — the point scorer's engine.

name: Karate
tagline: The empty hand way — Okinawa's art of one strike, one point.
overview: Karate — the way of the empty hand — is Okinawa's indigenous fighting tradition (blending Chinese quanfa with local te) codified into modern Japan's most exported martial art. It practices through three pillars: kihon (basics), kata (formal sequences preserving technique), and kumite (sparring), with sport karate's two Olympic disciplines being kata (demonstration judged) and kumite (point sparring to the clean decisive blow).

The art traveled from Okinawa's schools (Funakoshi's 1922 Tokyo demonstration seeding Shotokan) through Japan's universities to the world, organizing under the World Karate Federation (WKF) with hundreds of national federations. Its Olympic debut at Tokyo 2020 celebrated the art's homecoming; the sport's deepest nations — Japan, France, Spain, Turkey, Iran, Azerbaijan, and Egypt — trade world titles in kumite's electric, chess-like point fighting.

Newcomers should expect a class structure that is itself the pedagogy: basics, kata, and sparring rotate in every session, and the dojo's etiquette (bowing, the kun) is the art's moral frame. Point sparring rewards timing, distance, and the clean finishing technique (the ippon concept: one clean strike, one point) — one strike, one point — which makes karate's sport form as much a reaction game as a fighting art.

name: Taekwondo
tagline: The way of the foot and fist — kicks first, Olympic scoring, and lightning timing.
overview: Taekwondo — the way of the foot and fist — is Korea's national martial art, famous for its kicking arsenal (spinning, jumping, and fast linear kicks) and its Olympic sport form: electronic-body-armor sparring (kyorugi) where kicks to the head and body score instantly, plus poomsae (forms) as a judged discipline. The sport's essence is timing and range: three two-minute rounds of reactive, scoring-first combat where a head kick flips a match in one touch.

Unified in the 1950s from Korea's kwans (schools) — General Choi Hong Hi's Oh Do Kwan and the KTA's unification work — taekwondo organized internationally under the World Taekwondo federation (1973, as WTF) and reached the Olympics as a demonstration in 1988-92 and a medal sport from Sydney 2000. Korea's Kukkiwon certifies technique and black belts worldwide, and the WT's daedo-era electronic scoring turned the sport into a game of exquisite reaction and footwork.

Newcomers should expect kicking to be the curriculum's center: flexibility (hips, hamstrings) is trained daily, and the belt system (geup to dan) gives the journey its structure. Olympic-style sparring rewards control and speed over power — scoring is by clean contact with permitted techniques — making taekwondo one of the most accessible entry points into combat sports for young athletes.

name: Muay Thai
tagline: The art of eight limbs — fists, elbows, knees, shins, and the clinch that owns them all.
overview: Muay Thai is Thailand's national sport and the art of eight limbs: punches, elbows, knees, and shins — plus the clinch, where knee strikes and control decide close-range exchanges. Fought over five three-minute rounds to traditional music (the sarama), it combines the sport's Buddhist-temple origins, the wai kru ritual dance, and the most punishing conditioning culture in striking sports.

The art's modern code crystallized in the 1930s (rounds, gloves, and rings replacing the older muay boran rules), and its stadium culture — Bangkok's Rajadamnern (1945) and Lumpinee (1956) stadiums as the sport's Wimbledon — crowns champions whose names are national news. Internationally, muay thai anchors kickboxing's technical base, grows through IFMA's world championships and IOC-recognized federation status, and stars in ONE Championship's global broadcasts.

Newcomers should respect the shin: conditioning (bag work, pad rounds) builds the tool, and technique before power keeps knees and shins intact. The clinch is the art's hidden graduate school — learn it early, and the teep (push kick) is the art's distance manager.

name: Kickboxing
tagline: Boxing's hands, karate's legs — the global striking sport of K-1's legacy.
overview: Kickboxing is the global striking sport: boxing's hands combined with karate's and muay thai's kicks under rules that favor fast, judgeable action. Its modern flagship is the K-1 style — punches, kicks, and knees (no elbows, limited clinch) over three rounds — the format that built the sport's greatest era in Japan's Tokyo Dome and continues today through GLORY's world tour and ONE Championship's striking divisions.

The sport grew from 1960s karate fighters (Joe Lewis's full-contact experiments in America, Osamu Noguchi and the Japanese 'kickboxing' coinage) through the full-contact karate boom, into K-1's 1993 founding — which turned kickboxing into stadium spectacle with heavyweight legends (Aerts, Hoost, Bonjasky, Schilt) and the greatest tournament format in striking sports. GLORY (2012) inherited the crown, and the sport's two worlds (point-fighting semi-contact lineages and full-contact K-1 rules) coexist in one family.

Newcomers get the best of two worlds: boxing's hands teach first, low kicks (the art's great equalizer) teach second, and the combination game — punch-to-kick entries — is the sport's signature. Find a gym teaching dutch-style kickboxing (the K-1 lineage's technical school) and condition your shins early.

name: Mixed Martial Arts (MMA)
tagline: Everything, against everyone — the full-contact synthesis that settled sport's oldest argument.
origin: Brazil (vale tudo) & Japan · modern UFC 1993 · Unified Rules 2000-01
overview: MMA is the synthesis sport: striking (boxing, kickboxing, muay thai) and grappling (wrestling, jiu-jitsu, judo) combined under one ruleset in a fenced arena, won by knockout, submission, or judges' decision. It grew from Brazil's vale tudo tradition and Japan's shoot wrestling experiments into the Unified Rules era (2001), and the UFC's global rise made it the fastest-growing combat sport in history — where every older discipline meets its ultimate test.

The sport's arc runs from UFC 1's style-versus-style curiosity (Royce Gracie's jiu-jitsu proofs) through the athletic commission era to today's professional mainstream: unified weight classes, medical suspensions, and a broadcast economy that made Conor McGregor, Amanda Nunes, and Jon Jones household names. Beneath the UFC runs a deep ecosystem: ONE Championship's Asian empire, PFL's season format, Bellator's legacy, and the amateur/IMMAF pathway feeding the professional ranks.

Newcomers should build the base in layers: one striking art and one grappling art trained concurrently (boxing + BJJ or muay thai + wrestling), then MMA-specific transitions (takedown entries off strikes, ground-and-pound defense) layered on. The cage rewards the complete athlete, and the sport's gym culture — where every discipline's coach shares the floor — is its quiet achievement.

name: Fencing
tagline: Physical chess at 30 km/h — foil, épée, and sabre on the piste.
overview: Fencing is swordplay formalized into sport: three weapons — foil (thrusts to the torso, right-of-way rules), épée (thrusts anywhere, simultaneous double-touches possible), and sabre (cutting and thrusting above the waist) — fought on a narrow piste with electric scoring. It has been in every modern Olympics since 1896, and its essence is a duel of timing and geometry: attacks begin as distances close, parries answer, and ripostes land in the half-second the blade gives you.

The sport descends directly from European dueling culture — the Renaissance schools of Italy and France wrote the theory (Achille Marozzo to the French school), and the classical masters converted it into sport. Modern fencing's powers are France, Italy, Russia's lineage, Hungary (sabre's eternal house), Korea, and the USA's rising generation; the FIE governs world cups and world championships, and the weapon-specific rulebooks (especially sabre's simultaneity and foil's right-of-way) make fencing the most refereed of combat sports.

Newcomers should expect the sport's manners and its mathematics: distance, tempo, and blade work are learned as one subject. Start at a club with all three weapons tried (most fencers settle into one within months), learn footwork before blades, and trust the sport's kind aging curve — fencers compete at world level into their forties.

name: Sumo
tagline: Japan's national sport — push, throw, or force them out of the ring.
origin: Japan · ritual roots 1500+ years · modern honbasho era 1909
overview: Sumo is Japan's national sport: two rikishi (wrestlers) collide in a 4.55-meter dohyō (clay ring), and one wins by pushing the opponent out or making any part of them besides the soles of the feet touch the ground. Behind the massive physiques is explosive technique — the initial charge (tachi-ai), grip fights over the mawashi (belt), throws, pushes, and trips — compressed into matches that average under ten seconds.

Sumo's roots are ritual: Shinto purification ceremonies and imperial court performances (the sumai sechie of 700s-1100s) preceded the professional era, which stabilized with the Edo-period patronage and the modern honbasho (official tournaments) structure. Six honbasho a year (January, March, May, July, September, November), the banzuke (rankings bulletin), and the top division's makuuchi with its yokozuna (grand champions) form a sporting world as ritualized as it is competitive.

Newcomers should watch before judging: the tachi-ai's violence is tactical (the initial charge decides most matches), and the kimarite (winning techniques) catalogue — 82 recognized techniques plus non-technique wins — is a martial encyclopedia. Foreign fans find the sport's fastest-growing home online; Japan's stables (heya) train wrestlers in a communal life whose discipline is as much the sport as the bouts.

name: Sambo
tagline: The Soviet synthesis — jacket wrestling with the world's fastest throws.
overview: Sambo — from the Russian acronym SAMozashchita Bez Oruzhiya (self-defense without weapons) — is the Soviet Union's martial synthesis: judo's jacket throws, folk wrestling's leg attacks, and military close-combat fused into a sport codified in 1938. Sport sambo resembles jacket wrestling with fast leg reaps and a points game; combat sambo adds strikes and is the cage-ready cousin that produced Fedor Emelianenko and Khabib Nurmagomedov.

The art was created through the work of Vasili Oshchepkov (a judo black belt under Kano, later a purge victim) and Viktor Spiridonov (a disabled veteran's softer system), with Anatoly Kharlampiev championing its official recognition in 1938. Today the international federation (FIAS) governs sport and combat sambo world championships, Russian schools dominate, and the art's influence runs through MMA's greatest grapplers and military combatives worldwide.

Newcomers with a judo or wrestling base will feel at home: sambo's jacket grips reward judoka, its leg attacks reward wrestlers, and its kurtka (jacket) is the sport's great technical equalizer. Find a FIAS-affiliated club or a combat sambo gym, learn the safety-critical leglock progressions slowly, and enjoy the world's fastest-paced jacket grappling.

name: Kendo
tagline: The way of the sword — bamboo blades, armor, and the shout that scores.
overview: Kendo — the way of the sword — is Japanese swordsmanship as modern budo: two practitioners in armor (bōgu) strike with split bamboo swords (shinai) at four sanctioned targets (head, wrists, torso, throat), with every valid strike requiring ki-ken-tai-ichi — the unification of spirit (the kiai shout), sword, and body. Points are awarded by three referees by majority; matches are won by two points or at time.

Descended from kenjutsu (the samurai's battlefield sword schools), kendo was systematized for education and police training, formalized as modern sport post-war (the All Japan Kendo Federation, 1952), and today counts millions of practitioners worldwide. Its technique is shouted into existence — men (head), kote (wrist), dō (torso), tsuki (throat thrust) — and its etiquette (the rei before and after everything) is the art's spine.

Newcomers should expect the footwork and the shout before the sword: kendo's unique stamp is that every strike announces itself, and the first six months are spent learning stance, footwork, and basic strikes in the air before armor. The All Japan Kendo Championship's winners and the Kyoto taikai's atmosphere are the tradition's summit; the sport's global federations (FIK) hold world championships every few years.
